section.title: Friendship and Foresight
section.sectionRationale: Continuing the Hezekiah collection, 25:1 to 29:27, this chapter gathers proverbs on humility about tomorrow, the honest wounds of a true friend versus the false kisses of an enemy, and the foresight of a shepherd who knows the state of his flock before riches themselves prove fleeting.
section.thesis: Wisdom refuses to boast about tomorrow, welcomes the painful honesty of a true friend over the flattering kisses of an enemy, and tends carefully to what actually sustains life, since riches do not last forever but a well-known flock does.
section.frameNote: Four clusters: do not boast about tomorrow, and let another praise you; the wounds of a friend and the sweetness of counsel; the never-satisfied eye, and iron sharpening iron; know the state of your flocks, for riches are not forever.

verses.text: Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may bring.
Let another praise you, and not your own mouth, a stranger, and not your own lips.
A stone is heavy and sand is a burden, but aggravation from a fool outweighs them both.
Wrath is cruel and anger is like a flood, but who can withstand jealousy?
Better an open rebuke than love that is concealed.
The wounds of a {{ohev|friend}} are faithful, but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.
The soul that is full loathes honey, but to a hungry soul, any bitter thing is sweet.
Like a bird that strays from its nest is a man who wanders from his home.
Oil and incense bring joy to the heart, and the sweetness of a friend is counsel to the soul.
Do not forsake your friend or your father's friend, and do not go to your brother's house in the day of your calamity; better a neighbor nearby than a brother far away.
Be wise, my son, and bring joy to my heart, so that I can answer him who taunts me.
The prudent see danger and take cover; but the simple keep going and pay the penalty.
Take the garment of him who posts security for a stranger; get collateral if it is for a foreigner.
If one blesses his neighbor with a loud voice early in the morning, it will be counted to him as a curse.
A constant dripping on a rainy day and a contentious woman are alike,
restraining her is like holding back the wind or grasping oil with one's right hand.
As iron sharpens iron, so one man sharpens another.
Whoever tends a fig tree will eat its fruit, and he who looks after his master will be honored.
As water reflects the face, so the heart reflects the true man.
Sheol and Abaddon are never satisfied; so the eyes of man are never satisfied.
A crucible for silver and a furnace for gold, but a man is tested by the praise accorded him.
Though you grind a fool like grain with mortar and a pestle, yet his folly will not depart from him.

units.label: Know the state of your flocks

verses.text: Be sure to know the state of your flocks, and pay close attention to your herds;
for riches are not forever, nor does a crown endure to every generation.
When hay is removed and new growth appears and the grain from the hills is gathered,
the lambs will provide you with clothing, and the goats with the price of a field.
You will have plenty of goats' milk to feed you, food for your household and nourishment for your maidservants.

ohev.gloss: One who loves, a true friend. Verse 6 pairs the wounds of such a friend, painful but faithful, against the kisses of an enemy, pleasant but deceitful, teaching that real love sometimes hurts on the surface while flattery, however sweet, betrays underneath.

basic.context: This chapter mixes practical wisdom about humility, friendship, and foresight. It warns against boasting about a future no one controls, praises the painful honesty of a true friend over an enemy's flattering kiss, and closes with the down to earth counsel to know your flocks well, since riches, unlike careful stewardship, never last forever.
basic.hermeneutics: These proverbs describe how wise living generally works: humility about the future, welcoming honest correction, cultivating real friendship, and diligent stewardship of what sustains life. They are not formulas guaranteeing specific outcomes but patterns that consistently mark a wise life under God.
basic.originalLanguages: Ohev, one who loves, verse 6, names the true friend whose wounds are faithful even when they hurt, set against the kisses of an enemy, which flatter yet deceive. The chapter's repeated agricultural images, tending a fig tree, verse 18, knowing the state of flocks, verse 23, reflect the everyday rural world of ancient Israel where careful stewardship, not sudden wealth, secured a family's future.
basic.typology: The faithful wounds of a friend, verse 6, anticipate the piercing yet saving wounds of Christ, by whose stripes His people are healed, Isaiah 53:5. Iron sharpening iron, verse 17, foreshadows the mutual sanctification believers are called to in the body of Christ, spurring one another on toward love and good deeds, Hebrews 10:24.
basic.christ: Verse 6's faithful wounds of a friend point ultimately to Christ, whose wounds, unlike any merely human friend's, were not just faithful but redemptive, by His stripes we are healed, Isaiah 53:5, the deepest possible fulfillment of a friend's painful love doing us good. And verse 17's picture of iron sharpening iron anticipates the mutual sharpening believers are called to within the church, the body of Christ, spurring one another on to love and good works as together they are conformed to Him, Hebrews 10:24-25.
basic.god: God stands behind the warning against boasting about tomorrow, verse 1, since only He truly knows and holds the future securely. He also stands behind the deeper testing pictured in verse 21, where a crucible refines silver, but a person is refined by how he handles praise, showing that God cares as much about character under flattery as character under trial.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 53:5 fulfills the faithful wounds of a friend in verse 6. Hebrews 10:24-25 develops the mutual sharpening of iron in verse 17. James 4:13-16 echoes the warning against boasting about tomorrow in verse 1. Galatians 6:2 echoes the friendship and mutual burden-bearing commended throughout the chapter.
basic.oneStory: Proverbs 27 calls for humility about the future, honest friendship over flattering deception, and diligent care for what actually sustains life. This whole vision reaches its height in Christ, whose faithful wounds heal rather than merely correct, and in the church, His body, where believers sharpen one another into His likeness.

context.literary:
Proverbs 27 belongs to the stretch that opens with the note of 25:1 and runs to 29:27, and within it the chapter reads as a loose necklace with a deliberate clasp. The opening pair of sayings sets the temper: verse 1 forbids boasting about a future no one owns, and verse 2 forbids praising yourself. Both are about who is entitled to speak a verdict on you. Time speaks last on tomorrow, and a stranger, not your own lips, should speak on your worth.

The middle of the chapter is stitched by sound and theme rather than argument. Verses 5 to 10 gather around friendship, with the word for friend or neighbour recurring, and they frame it with two food pictures: the full soul that loathes honey, verse 7, and the sweetness of a friend's counsel, verse 9. Verses 15 and 16 pair a dripping roof with a quarrelsome spouse, and verse 17 immediately answers the strain of a bad household with the strength of a good friendship, iron on iron. Verses 20 and 21 form a hinge: the grave is never full, the eye is never full, and the only thing that proves a person is how he carries praise.

The close, verses 23 to 27, is the longest single thought in the chapter and changes register. After a run of one line sayings, the teacher slows into a small farming poem with a clear sequence: know your flock, because wealth is fleeting, then follow the seasons of hay, new growth and mountain grain, to the lambs, the goats and the milk. The poem begins with a command and ends with a household fed, so the chapter finishes with a picture of enough rather than a warning.
context.historical:
The chapter's world is the hill country of Judah, where a household lived by sheep and goats, a fig tree by the door, and small plots watered by rain. Wool and kid gave clothing and ready cash, verse 26, and the price of a field came from the flock, which tells us land was bought from the proceeds of animals, not the other way round. Goat's milk, verse 27, was the daily staple. A shepherd who did not know the condition of each animal lost wealth quietly: a lame ewe, a missed lambing, a poor pasture.

The warning about kings in verse 24 would have landed hard in a society whose memory held the break of Solomon's house and the short, bloody dynasties of the northern kingdom. A crown was never guaranteed to the next generation, which is exactly the point.

Verses 10 and 13 reflect village life under obligation. A man in calamity naturally runs to his brother, but verse 10 observes that a brother may live two days away while a neighbour is at the gate. Surety, verse 13, was a real danger: a man who guaranteed a stranger's loan could lose the cloak on his back, and the same line appears in Proverbs 20:16, so the editors evidently thought it worth repeating. The repeated sayings about the quarrelsome wife and the dripping roof, verses 15 and 16, echo Proverbs 19:13 and 25:24, and recall flat Palestinian roofs of beaten clay that leaked in the winter rains.

Sheol and Abaddon, verse 20, are the realm of the dead as Israel pictured it, a place to which everyone goes and which is never full.
context.canonical:
Proverbs 27 is quoted far less than it is echoed. James 4:13 to 16 is the nearest New Testament parallel to verse 1, taking the merchant who plans a year of profit and reminding him that life is a mist. Jesus' parable of the rich fool, Luke 12:16 to 21, puts a name and a night on the same truth: a man who counted on many years and was asked for his life before dawn.

The wounds of a friend find a sibling in Psalm 141:5, where the psalmist asks that a righteous man strike him and calls the rebuke loving devotion and oil for his head, so verse 6 here and the oil of verse 9 meet in a single psalm. Galatians 6:1 supplies the posture of the one who wounds: a spirit of gentleness, and a warning to watch yourself.

Verse 20 pairs Sheol with human desire, and Ecclesiastes 1:8 and 4:8 carry the thought into the Preacher's long inquiry, while Habakkuk 2:5 compares the arrogant man's appetite to Sheol. Abaddon is picked up in Revelation 9:11 as the name of the angel of the abyss. The shepherd poem prepares the way for Ezekiel 34, where bad shepherds feed themselves and neglect the flock, and for John 10:14, where the Good Shepherd says He knows His sheep. Verse 17 stands behind the believer's mutual duties in Hebrews 10:24 and 25.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The teacher is training a young man to be the sort of person others can safely rely on and the sort who does not need to be managed. The first lesson is that a human life is lived in two directions, towards time and towards people, and both require humility. Not knowing the day is no excuse for despair, it is a reason to plan modestly and to leave room for God. Not being able to see your own face is a reason to want friends who tell the truth.

Behind these lessons stands a concern for the first hearers' homes. A father who says, verse 11, that his son's wisdom lets him answer a taunter is thinking of reputation in a village, where a foolish son shames the whole house. The father wants the son to resist the sort of dependence that flattery breeds, to choose and keep the friend of the family, verse 10, and to give daily and unglamorous attention to the thing that actually feeds the household.

The closing poem is meant to be heard as a promise as well as a command. Attention to the flock is what turns a fragile prosperity, verse 24, into steady provision, verses 26 and 27. The editor wants the hearer to be neither anxious about wealth that cannot be held nor careless about the work that sustains a family.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Most of this chapter describes what is observed in life and recommends a response; very little of it is a command in the strict sense. The direct imperatives are narrow: do not boast, verse 1, do not forsake your friend, verse 10, be wise, verse 11, take the garment of the surety, verse 13, and know your flocks, verse 23. The rest are comparisons and observations that the hearer is meant to absorb.

That matters for the sayings that sound harsh. The lines about the quarrelsome woman, verses 15 and 16, are an observation about the misery of a household at odds, repeated from earlier in the book, and they are not a verdict on women or a rule for marriage. Proverbs 31 will soon set the praise of a capable wife beside them. The advice to take a stranger's cloak, verse 13, is about the prudence of a lender, not a commendation of hard dealing.

What carries forward is the shape of the wise life. We can still refuse to put our confidence in tomorrow, accept a friend's hard word, and look hard at the real state of whatever has been entrusted to us. We should not treat verse 8 as a ban on leaving home, or verse 24 as promising that careful people never lose their wealth.

debates.question: Does verse 6, 'better an open rebuke than love that is concealed,' teach that all criticism, however delivered, should be welcomed as a mark of true friendship?

views.label: Any rebuke, however harsh, proves greater love than silence
views.case: The stark contrast between a friend's wounds and an enemy's kisses could be read as valuing bluntness itself, regardless of tone or manner, over any withheld criticism.

views.label: The verse commends honest, well-meant correction motivated by love, not harshness for its own sake
views.case: The Hebrew parallel is between 'faithful' wounds, verse 6, meaning trustworthy and well-intentioned, and mere flattery; Proverbs elsewhere prizes gentle, well-timed speech, 25:11 and 15:1, so the point is honesty rooted in genuine care, not license for cruelty dressed up as friendship.

debates.bearing: Read alongside the rest of Proverbs' concern for gentle, well-timed speech, the proverb commends honest correction offered out of real love, not harshness excused as honesty; the test is the friend's faithfulness and motive, not merely the sting of the words.

debates.question: What does verse 21 mean when it says a man is tested by the praise accorded him?

views.label: He is tested by the praise he receives
views.case: The line sits right after the crucible and furnace, which reveal the quality of metal. Praise functions as a furnace for the person praised: some are puffed up and show their pride, some stay humble. This fits verses 1 and 2, which warn against self praise and welcome the praise of a stranger.

views.label: He is tested by what he praises
views.case: The Hebrew is brief and literally speaks of a man according to his praise, which can mean the praise given by him as well as to him. On this view, what a person admires, a clever scoundrel or a faithful friend, discloses his own character, as the company he keeps does in verse 19.

views.label: He is tested by how he responds to praise or flattery
views.case: A third reading folds the two together: the test is the response. Flattery has been named as the enemy's kiss in verse 6, and the wise man receives praise without letting it guide him.

debates.bearing: The first reading best fits the surrounding verses and is what most translations adopt, but the others are not far from it. All three agree that praise is dangerous precisely because it feels pleasant, and that character shows in how a person handles it.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 begins with the verb for boasting in the reflexive stem, a form that means to praise oneself, and it is the same root as the word for praise in verse 2 and in the praise of verse 21. The chapter is built around this one root: do not praise yourself, let another praise you, and learn what praise does to you. The second half of verse 1 says literally that you do not know what a day will bring forth, using the verb for giving birth. Time is pictured as a womb, and tomorrow as an unborn child whose nature no one can predict.

Verse 23 begins with a doubled form of the verb to know, the infinitive set beside the finite verb, so that it means something like know, really know, the state of your flocks. The word for state is literally the face of the flock, the condition you read as you read a face. Verse 19 uses the same word for face twice: as water reflects the face, so the heart reflects the man. The chapter treats faces as what honest looking reveals, which is why verse 17, in the Hebrew, says that one man sharpens the face of another, as the BSB footnote records. Friendship is not a vague influence, it is a mirror held up at close range.

The word for the faithful wounds of verse 6 is built on the root of amen, trustworthy and reliable. A wound is called faithful when it can be trusted to mean well, and the deceit of the enemy's kisses is contrasted not with gentleness but with reliability. In verse 9, the oil and incense that gladden the heart belong to the world of perfume and the sanctuary, so the counsel of a friend is honoured with the most delightful thing a hearer could name.

Sheol and Abaddon in verse 20 form a pair: Abaddon, from the root meaning to perish, appears in Job 26:6 and 28:22 and Proverbs 15:11 as a poetic name for the place of the dead. It is rendered Destruction or Death and Destruction in the BSB footnote. The Greek form of the name appears in Revelation 9:11.

Verse 24 says that riches are not forever and then adds that nor does a crown endure to every generation. The Hebrew idiom for every generation is a doubled phrase, literally to generation and generation, a phrase Israel also used in praise of the LORD's reign, as in Psalm 146:10. Kings come and go, and God is the only one who does not.

typology.fulfillment: The friend whose wounds are faithful is a pattern of Christ, who loved to the point of being wounded and who told hard truths to people He loved. He said to the rich young ruler what no flatterer would, Mark 10:21, and rebuked Peter in the same breath as He loved him, Matthew 16:23. The escalation is that Christ took the wound upon Himself: He was pierced for our transgressions and by His stripes we are healed, Isaiah 53:5. A human friend can wound only with words. Christ's wounds remove the sin the words exposed. The type falls short wherever a human friend is mistaken or proud.

typology.type: The friend who stays closer than a brother, Proverbs 27:10 and 18:24
typology.fulfillment: Verse 10 prefers a nearby neighbour to a distant brother, and the book elsewhere speaks of a friend who stays closer than a brother, Proverbs 18:24. Jesus fills this out when He tells His disciples that He no longer calls them servants but friends, because He has made known to them everything He learned from the Father, John 15:15. Abraham was called a friend of God, Isaiah 41:8, but in Christ the friendship is bought at the cost of His life, John 15:13. The type falls short because every human friend dies or fails to be present on the day of calamity, and Christ does neither, Matthew 28:20.

typology.type: The shepherd who knows his flock, Proverbs 27:23
typology.fulfillment: Knowing the condition of every animal in the flock is the work of the shepherd, and Scripture gives that picture to the Lord Himself, Psalm 23:1. Jesus claims it for Himself: 'I am the good shepherd. I know My sheep and My sheep know Me,' John 10:14. Where the farmer of Proverbs guards his herd for the sake of his own profit, the Good Shepherd lays down His life for the sheep, John 10:11. Ezekiel 34 condemns shepherds who feed themselves, and Peter calls elders to tend the flock willingly and promises the Chief Shepherd's unfading crown, 1 Peter 5:2 to 4. The type is limited, since the farmer is a man guarding his property.

typology.type: The crown that does not endure, Proverbs 27:24
typology.fulfillment: Verse 24 observes that no crown lasts to every generation. Christ is the king whose crown does last: the angel promised that He would reign over the house of Jacob forever and that His kingdom would never end, Luke 1:33. The throne of David, so often lost in Israel's history, is established forever in Him, as 2 Samuel 7:13 promised. In Revelation 19:12 the risen Lord wears many crowns. The type works by contrast, since the proverb states what no human crown can do and Christ is the one who does it.

study.christ:
This chapter leads to Christ most plainly through its two great pictures of relationship: the friend whose wounds are faithful and the shepherd who knows his flock. Together they sketch what a person needs most and cannot provide for himself, a companion who will tell the truth at cost to himself, and a keeper who knows him by name.

Consider the friend first. The sort of friendship verse 6 praises is rare because it is expensive. The friend has to risk the friendship to preserve the person. In Jesus this is unmistakable. He told the rich young man the one thing he lacked, and Mark adds that He looked at him and loved him, Mark 10:21. He turned on Peter with the hardest words in the Gospels, Matthew 16:23, moments after praising him. Yet the most faithful wound He ever bore was not given to a friend but received for enemies. 'While we were still sinners, Christ died for us,' Romans 5:8. The enemy's kisses of verse 6 find their sharpest illustration in Judas, who betrayed Him with a kiss, Luke 22:47 and 48, and the faithful wounds in the One who accepted it.

Then the shepherd. Proverbs tells a farmer to know the face of his flock, and the New Testament says that is what Christ does. 'I know My sheep and My sheep know Me,' John 10:14. Where the proverb says riches and crowns are not forever, Jesus names the rich fool who planned barns and lost his life that night, Luke 12:20, and then tells His disciples not to be afraid, little flock, since the Father has been pleased to give them the kingdom, Luke 12:32. The two halves of verse 24 are answered in Him: the treasure in heaven does not fail, Luke 12:33, and His kingdom has no end, Luke 1:33.

Verse 1 teaches the posture that Jesus modelled in Gethsemane. He did not boast about tomorrow but asked, not as I will, but as You will, Matthew 26:39. James turns the same instinct into a rule for His people, If the Lord is willing, James 4:15.

A caution keeps this honest. Proverbs 27 is not a hidden gospel, and the iron of verse 17 is not a code for Christ. The chapter points forward because it describes the needs, a true friend and a faithful keeper, that He alone fully meets.
study.god:
Verse 1 sets up the God of the chapter by implication. If no one knows what a day may bring, then someone does, and the book of Proverbs says plainly who it is: many are the plans in a human heart, but the counsel of the LORD stands, Proverbs 19:21. The command not to boast is therefore a form of worship. It declines to take the place of the One who holds the future, and it frees the hearer from the exhausting task of securing it.

The chapter also shows a God who uses ordinary means. The friend whose counsel is sweet, verse 9, the neighbour who comes when a brother is far away, verse 10, and the furnace of public praise, verse 21, are the instruments of formation. God has not left the shaping of character to private visions. He arranges that we should be sharpened by one another, and whoever rejects that arrangement will stay dull.

It shows a God whose attention is detailed. The farming poem asks a man to know the state of each animal in the flock. The Bible regularly pictures God Himself as that shepherd: He tends His flock like a shepherd and gathers the lambs in His arms, Isaiah 40:11. Such a God cares about lambs, goats' milk and a maidservant's food, verse 27, and the chapter ends on household provision, not on a lofty abstraction.

Verse 20 holds a tension worth naming. Sheol and the eyes of man share a hunger that nothing in creation can fill, and the book gives the cure in other places, where the fear of the LORD leads to life, and one rests satisfied, untouched by harm, Proverbs 19:23. The God of Proverbs 27 does not shame our wanting, but redirects it.

Finally, the chapter reveals the character of God by contrast with the flatterer. God rebukes those He loves, Proverbs 3:12 and Hebrews 12:6, and does not flatter. For worship, this means we can bring our boasting, our loneliness and our hunger to a God who tells us the truth and stays near.

crossReferences.note: The nearest New Testament parallel to verse 1. James takes the planner who intends to spend a year in a city making a profit, reminds him that he does not know what tomorrow holds, and calls life a mist. His remedy, 'If the Lord is willing,' turns the proverb's prohibition into a prayerful habit.

The parable of the rich fool is verse 1 and verse 24 in story form. A harvest, bigger barns, and a plan for many years are met by a voice that asks for his life that night. Jesus draws the conclusion that riches stored for oneself are not riches toward God.

A psalmist who asks to be struck by the righteous and calls the rebuke loving devotion and oil for the head. It supplies the inner attitude that verse 6 requires of the one wounded, and it ties together the wound of verse 6 and the oil of verse 9.

The manner in which a faithful wound should be given. Someone caught in a trespass is to be restored with a spirit of gentleness, and the rebuker is to watch himself. It guards verse 6 against turning into permission to be harsh.

Almost identical to verse 13, in the sayings of Solomon collected earlier. The repetition across two collections shows how the editors treated surety as a standing danger, and warns that a man who guarantees a stranger's debt may lose his cloak.

Speaks of a friend who stays closer than a brother, set against a man of many companions who comes to ruin. It is a natural companion to verse 10, which also ranks the neighbour who is near above the brother who is far, and it keeps friendship tied to faithfulness rather than numbers.

The eye is not satisfied with seeing, in the Preacher's opening survey of toil. It carries the thought of verse 20 into a whole book that asks where a hungry eye can find rest, and answers it in the fear of God.

The first of the proverbs about a quarrelsome wife like constant dripping, repeated here in verses 15 and 16 and in Proverbs 25:24. It shows that this chapter gathers from a stock of sayings the editors knew well.

The Good Shepherd lays down His life for the sheep and knows them by name. It takes verse 23, where a man must know the state of his flock, and shows the Lord doing it at a cost the farmer never paid.

Believers are to consider how to spur one another on to love and good deeds and not to neglect meeting together. This is the community application of verse 17: iron sharpens iron only when two pieces are brought into contact.

Elders are to shepherd the flock of God willingly, not for gain, and the Chief Shepherd will give the crown of glory that will never fade away. The unfading crown answers the crown of verse 24 that does not last.
He tends His flock like a shepherd, gathering the lambs in His arms. The Lord Himself does what verse 23 asks of a farmer, and the comfort of the picture shows why the chapter can end on provision.

study.oneStory:
Proverbs 27 sits in the long stretch of the Bible that asks how fragile creatures should live under a good Creator in a world that has been bent. It answers what Genesis 3 left open on the human side: now that the first pair have hidden from God and from one another, how do people recover the honest face-to-face that Eden began with? Verse 19 says that the heart reflects the man as water reflects the face, and the whole chapter is a lesson in being truly seen. The friend's rebuke, the neighbour at the gate and the shepherd who reads each animal's face are the means by which a world of hiding is slowly repaired.

The chapter also faces the curse on the ground. Genesis 3:17 to 19 promised that bread would come by toil, and the farm poem of verses 23 to 27 is the quiet gospel of that sentence: work still feeds a household, the seasons still turn, and lambs, goats and milk are real grace. The Bible never pretends this is permanent. Riches pass and crowns fall, verse 24, and Sheol is never full, verse 20.

The story moves on to a shepherd king. David came from the sheepfolds, and the prophets rebuke the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves, Ezekiel 34:2. God promises to shepherd His sheep Himself and to set over them one shepherd, His servant David, Ezekiel 34:23. Jesus claims to be that shepherd and the friend who lays down His life, John 10:11 and 15:13. In Him a crown does endure to every generation, Luke 1:33.

At the end of the story the hungry eye is satisfied. The Lamb on the throne will be their shepherd and will guide them to springs of living water, Revelation 7:17, and there will be no more Sheol, for death and Hades are thrown into the lake of fire, Revelation 20:14. The friendship begun in a garden is completed in a city where God's servants will see His face, Revelation 22:4.

sermon.title: Friendship
sermon.why: Preached at Redeemer Presbyterian Church on May 29, 2005 in the series Proverbs: True Wisdom for Living, this sermon works directly from Proverbs 27:5-6, 9, 14, and 17, among other friendship texts, describing the marks of a true friend, constancy, carefulness, candor, and counsel, and grounding the capacity for real friendship in the friendship of Jesus shown at the cross.

options.text: Boasting about tomorrow, since you do not know what a day may bring.
options.note: The uncertainty of the future should produce humility, not presumptuous boasting.

options.text: Making any plans at all for the future.
options.note: The verse warns against boastful presumption, not planning itself.

options.text: Speaking about the past.
options.note: The verse's concern is tomorrow, not the past.

options.text: Sharing your plans with close friends.
options.note: The warning is against arrogant boasting, not simply discussing plans with trusted friends.

quiz.q: What does verse 6 say about the wounds of a friend compared to the kisses of an enemy?

options.text: The friend's wounds are faithful, but the enemy's kisses are deceitful.
options.note: Painful honesty from someone who loves you is more trustworthy than pleasant flattery from someone who does not.

options.text: Both are equally trustworthy expressions of care.
options.note: The verse draws a sharp contrast, not an equivalence.

options.text: The enemy's kisses are more valuable since they are pleasant.
options.note: This reverses the verse's clear point.

options.text: Wounds from anyone, friend or enemy, should always be trusted.
options.note: The verse specifically distinguishes a friend's faithful wounds from an enemy's deceitful kisses, not wounds from any source.

quiz.q: What does verse 17 say about how people affect one another?

options.text: As iron sharpens iron, so one man sharpens another.
options.note: Close relationships can refine and improve character through mutual influence.

options.text: People have no real effect on one another's character.
options.note: This is the opposite of the verse's point.

options.text: Iron is used only as a metaphor for wealth in this verse.
options.note: The metaphor is about sharpening and mutual influence, not wealth.

options.text: Only teachers can sharpen students, not peers.
options.note: The verse's image, one man sharpening another, suggests mutual peer influence, not a one-directional teacher-student relationship exclusively.

quiz.q: What does verse 20 say about human eyes?

options.text: Like Sheol and Abaddon, they are never satisfied.
options.note: Human desire is pictured as insatiable, like the realm of the dead that never has enough.

options.text: They are easily satisfied with modest possessions.
options.note: This is the opposite of the verse's claim.

options.text: They are satisfied only by great wealth.
options.note: The verse suggests an inherent insatiability, not a threshold that, once reached, brings satisfaction.

options.text: They become more easily satisfied with age.
options.note: The verse makes no claim about satisfaction changing with age; the point is a persistent, ongoing lack of satisfaction.

quiz.q: Why does verse 23-24 urge knowing the state of your flocks?

options.text: Because riches are not forever, nor does a crown endure to every generation.
options.note: Diligent stewardship matters precisely because wealth is not automatically permanent.

options.text: Because flocks are more valuable than money.
options.note: The comparison is about permanence and diligence, not relative value of assets.

options.text: Because riches, once gained, last forever automatically.
options.note: This is the opposite of what the text explicitly states.

options.text: Because it is a purely sentimental, non-practical suggestion.
options.note: The passage frames this as practical wisdom tied to real economic survival, not mere sentiment.

questions: Verse 1 warns against boasting about tomorrow. Where have you been presuming on a future that is not actually guaranteed to you?
Verse 6 says a friend's wounds are more trustworthy than an enemy's kisses. Who in your life loves you enough to tell you a hard truth, and how do you usually respond when they do?
Iron sharpens iron, verse 17. Who is sharpening you right now, and who are you being called to sharpen?
Verse 20 says human eyes are never satisfied. Where in your own life is more never actually enough, and what would contentment look like there?

Verse 23 calls for knowing the state of your flocks rather than presuming on wealth. What area of your life, finances, health, relationships, needs more attentive, ongoing care rather than passive assumption?

translationNotes.note: 'Faithful' translates ne'emanim, the same root behind 'amen,' meaning trustworthy, reliable, firm, contrasting sharply with the deceit of an enemy's kiss.
'Grasping oil with one's right hand' pictures something inherently ungraspable, oil slipping through fingers, applied here to the futility of trying to restrain a contentious spirit by force.
'Sheol and Abaddon' name the realm and the place of destruction associated with death, both personified here as insatiable, paralleling the endless appetite of human desire.
